utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, the Chamber would like to explain to the parties that it did its utmost best to see whether we could give some guidance to the parties and so that they would be better aware of what in the 92 ter statement we would consider to admit and what not. We started also going through all of the annexes. We couldn't finish that, also because the Judges had quite a lot of other things on their agenda as well which was urgent, both today and yesterday. But for guidance, as far as matters stand now, the Prosecution is informed that - and I am focusing on the 92 ter statement for the next witness - Mr. Re, I do understand no protective measures? - Mr. Stijovic would be that paragraph 21; 39; 40, the first five lines; 59, last six lines; and now I jump a bit back again, 11 to and including 16; paragraph 17; and paragraph 26 are not suitable for being admitted under Rule 92 ter. Then there is a second category where the Chamber indicates that it sees no reason at this moment to deny admission of these paragraphs but the put the Prosecution at notice that the level of sourcing is such that in order to use this material in evidence as you likely will have it on your mind, Mr. Re, it certainly needs further elaboration, which, of course, can elicit it from the witness when he testifies. That would be: Paragraphs 20; 23; 24; 25, first nine lines; 27; 32, first nine lines; 36; 37, first six lines; 41, first fifteen lines; paragraph 50, lines 9 to 11; 54; and 58, first four lines. Of course, in these paragraphs, often reference is made to annexes where the Chamber indicates that further elaboration may be needed. This might have an impact on the admission of annexes referred to in these paragraphs. Sometimes where the witness mainly repeats or refers to what we find in the annexes, it may be clear that the fate of the admission of the annexes might be related to the level of elaboration that is achieved. The Chamber will continue working on it. The Chamber not realistically expects the testimony of this witness to be concluded today. Therefore, tomorrow and over the weekend we might have more time to give more detailed guidance to the parties. I thought it would be wise to start with this. Any other procedural issues at this moment to be raised? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Clarification, please, of the ruling in relation to paragraph 20. Paragraph 20 starts on page 11 in the English and goes right through to page 17. It's divided (a) to (t).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 20 -- of course, if you look at the-- some of the annexes are not objected to by the Defence, but then in the limited sense, that the Defence says we -- whether authentic or not, we do not oppose admission for very limited purposes. Therefore, I think the -- but let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have earlier discussed the matter. It is mainly the indication that further elaboration is needed is primarily applicable to the first paragraph, where the witness introduces his own statistics and where I think the Defence argued that this was just copying from other sources, rather than any personal knowledge of the witness. So therefore sourcing of that material might need further attention. When I refer to the remainder of it, that is, the long list of events described which are outside the time scope of the indictment, there the Defence, although for limited purposes, does not object the admission of the annexes. Of course, the -- the relevance of that material is limited. Mr. Re, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, but if I could just have a moment to highlight in different colours the effect of the ruling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- so I can lead the witness appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you need for that or --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A few minutes. If I could just go in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we already invite Madam Usher to call the witness in. That usually takes some time. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is it the first nine lines of 25 or the first nine lines of 27? Could I ask that. And then it says first nine lines afterwards. I'm just a bit unclear which the first nine lines are referring to in each of those ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 25, the first nine lines. Then paragraph 27 in its entirety. And then 32, again first nine lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stijovic. My apologies for not paying proper attention to you entering the courtroom. Mr. Stijovic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stijovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Re, who's counsel for the Prosecution. But he needs one more second to write a few things down. Mr. Re, otherwise perhaps I can start. Is your name Zoran Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is your date of birth the 13th day of November, 1962?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We didn't receive an answer to the first question, but I take it that I -- I mentioned your correct name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you born in Podgorica, Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, I'm going to show you a statement dated the 26th of September, 2007. Do you have a -- I want to show it to you in hard copy. That will be 65 ter 2006 -- I'm sorry, 2066.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If this could be perhaps shown to the witness in its entirety in hard copy, it might be quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hear no objection by the Defence, so ... Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber refrains at this moment from deciding upon -- deciding the admission of this -- of this statement. Mr. Re, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First, I have several questions to ask you in relation to that statement. Firstly, is it accurate? Does it bear your declaration? That is, the 37 pages in Serbian in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And secondly, if I or the Judges or the Defence were to ask you about the matters in there, is that the evidence you would give if we asked you those questions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I note that it's been given an exhibit number already, but on that basis, may it be tendered into -- received into evidence subject to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Subject to later rulings about submission, yes. Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. The -- you were talking about the statement of the 26th of September, I think you said. Yes. Now, I see that the witness acknowledgment in the English language is dated the 26th; however, the original seems to be the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It seems to have been signed on the 27th. That's my error.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please just go to the last page, Mr. Stijovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's important that it's on the record. And if I don't hear anything from the Defence, then I take it it's the same statement and that there could be no confusion as far as the date is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've given the witness a copy of the 35 of the 75 annexes in Serbian or Albanian which I intend to take him through during the course of his evidence. I haven't got the complete binder there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, before you came into court, the Court made some rulings about some particular passages in your statement which will not be received into evidence. I'm going to ask you some questions about some of the matters, but others I -- I won't. I haven't had a chance to highlight those which are in and which are out. We'll have to give you a copy later during one of the breaks where we've actually highlighted the parts which will -- will not be received into evidence. Do you -- do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 2, you refer to working in the Serbian State Security and being the head of the analytical section in Pristina in -- from 1995 onwards. How senior was that position within the Serbian State Security at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of hierarchy, it was a very important position, given that all internal data that was at the disposal of the State Security Service was at my disposal; that is also because of my professional position and it all gave me a fairly good view from which I could monitor the events that were developing in Kosovo, particularly on the part of the KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army. In terms of hierarchy, the department of analysis is a separate unit receiving all data and information received by the State Security Service through its operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you say whereabouts you were in the hierarchy? One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or wherever?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The fourth or the fifth person.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your level or your security classification? How high was that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've tried to explain. The State Security Service of Serbia organised -- or rather, organises its operation in terms of territory and professional distribution. In that system, the analysis department is a separate unit, streamlining all of the data sent in by other operational units. Everything that is done according to the territorial and professional distribution, it all goes to the analysis department. It is the only part of the State Security Service where one can find all information concerning the State Security Service's operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we take from that you had access to absolutely everything that passed through the office, or were there things that were too secret for even you to see?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This department was something that fell within the scope of my competence, and I was able to see it. There may have been certain operational issues and things which remained at the operational level at a certain point in time. But as time went by, again such information would find its way in the course of operational work to the analytical department.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we might at this juncture just for purposes of clarity of the record perhaps have some inquiry into what "operational level" and "operational issues" means so that we know where we're proceeding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I -- I leave it up to you whether you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sure. It's a fair query.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith wants to know what "operational level" and "operational issues" mean. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Operational situation" is a given situation within which the State Security Service wants to secure the achievement of a certain goal. For example, in this case, it was monitoring the operation of the KLA and trying to hinder their operations as possible -- as much as possible, as well as to try and prevent certain individual activities on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I was after in my earlier question was the level of security clearance you had. You know, in a -- a security system there are different levels of clearance according to your seniority and what you're allowed to see. Can you just briefly explain whether -- where you fitted in in terms of what you had access to. I just wasn't quite clear from your earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: My security clearance was equal to that of the inner circle, of the very few people that had all of the data at their disposal. The analytical department had more information, as a matter of fact, than operational leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, how did your level of security clearance compare to, say, the Minister of Interior or the Chief of Military Intelligence or the President of the Republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, concerning the operations of the State Security Service in Kosovo and Metohija, based on the information we had following the State Security line, we would inform the leadership; in this specific case, the President of the Republic and the Ministry of the Interior. We also informed the top state leadership on the current issue, in keeping with the procedure that was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the strength of the State Security in Kosovo in 1998? I mean, how many people were employed by State Security approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I can be specific, given the limitations concerning the organisation and methodology of the service; however, I can say that in terms of numbers concerning active-duty operatives within the State Security Service, that figure was over 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are operatives employees of the service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Operational officers are operatives of the Security Service, but it also includes people of other profiles, like analysts, technicians, and so on and so forth. But that's where I would stop describing the individual activities conducted by the State Security. What I had in mind were people in full employment, active-duty employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about people providing information to the State Security Service? What sort of figures are we talking about there? Across Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The same applies. I believe I am limited as to the extent of my answer to this question. However, I'll try to put it in a framework. Given the amount of information we received and the type of it during 1998, the State Security Service in Kosovo identified over 200 insiders within the structures where Albanian extremists moved. There were several hundred people in Kosovo who were our human sources, so to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, may I interrupt for one second. Could you and could the Defence please also look at page 9, line 3, 4, and 5, where the testimony of the witness is not reflected in the transcript. Now, I can imagine that the follow-up questions sufficiently cover the matter, so therefore I'm asking the parties whether they would prefer to have the witness to repeat that answer or whether we could just move on and consider that what was asked is sufficiently dealt with in the follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My understanding of the answers that precede and follow the absent passage is that the witness has testified that all information flowed through the analytical department at one time or another. In other words, all information available within the RDB from an operational level upwards at one time or another passed through the analytical department. And it's on that basis that I've understood his testimony. If that's wrong, then obviously a correction is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps he could -- he could confirm that representation and see whether that's an accurate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you may not have noticed that there was a small portion of your answer that was not received by the transcribers. Mr. Emmerson now explained how I understood your testimony in this respect. If you would agree with that. And please, could you say aloud "yes" or "no," because nodding doesn't appear on the transcript. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no need to have the witness repeat those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm also wondering with regard to the answer the witness gave prior to this one, he indicated he was somewhat limited. And I don't know whether or not that's because some directions had been received or a failure of memory or information. I don't know what that meant precisely. And perhaps Mr. Re could -- could inquire into that so we keep a constant flow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- if -- if Mr. Re is happy with the answers of the witness -- now he said he can, and I take it that he will. Next time perhaps if Mr. Re is happy with the answer, only if it really leads to -- to total lack of understanding of the -- of the testimony, that the Defence asks for clarification. Otherwise, seeks clarification in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The answer was in the context of the number of individuals who were giving information to the RDB, so I thought it might be something worthwhile to pursue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, is there anything in your saying a moment ago "I believe I am limited as to the extent of my answer." And if so, please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing of importance, I believe. It may be important, though, to know that I am free to address state and security secrets if they fall within the scope of crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija. As for the organisation and methodology of the State Security Service, I cannot discuss that area in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, if at any moment you -- your answer, in view of what you just said, would not reflect not only the truth but would not reflect the whole truth, would you please tell us then that at that moment that you are not giving the details because you feel not free to do so. What the Chamber then will do is another matter, but that we are at least aware where your answer is less complete than it would be without these limitation you -- limitations you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I wish to make it absolutely clear that for the purposes of cross-examination that is the very area which I wish to penetrate; in other words, the methodology of the RDB and associated services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. We'll come to that, and then Mr. Stijovic will tell us where he has difficulties in giving the full answer to the questions, and then we'll see how to proceed. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, of course in your statement you've actually referred to what I think we may describe as the methodology of the way the State Security Service operated. And bearing that in mind, I'll just take you back to the last answer before that discussion, which was, to remind you, you said: "Given the amount of information we received and the type of it in -- during 1998, we identified over 200 insiders within the structures where Albanian extremists moved. There were several hundred people in Kosovo who were our human sources, so to say." I just want to ask you about the definition of the structures where Albanian extremists moved. Are you referring to the KLA or other organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Since I also provided a statement about the activities of the KLA and Albanian extremists, this is what I had in mind, that structure and their activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could you please slow down a bit, because the interpreters have problems. I wasn't listening to the other channel, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is another way of expressing that that you had 200 people within the KLA who were providing the DB with information in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: One could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And at what levels of the KLA were these people operating? Referring to -- from top to bottom. Whereabouts were these people within it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I can answer to that question this way: If we are talking about the area of Metohija, we had our man in our headquarters. He worked for the State Security Service. We also had our people in other areas, and we were able to reach as high as the level of headquarters. Our insiders would then notify us on the activities of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Line 24, "in their headquarters."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you talking General Staff, at the top? Or are you talking about headquarters at different levels? I want you to clarify that so we know exactly where your informers were, at what level of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: At the highest level. What may be important is to say that we had very good information on KLA activities in the staffs in the rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Because I know what information passed through my hands. I received reports from collaborators. Those people covertly worked and they were working for the State Security Service in secret. Through the reports I received, within the total amount of information, I could gather that those people were highly positioned and that they were at the very top of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were you able to assess the reliability of the information that these people were giving to the Serbian State Security?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian State Security Service, just as in other similar organisations, there is a methodology, a methodology on how to classify and how to verify the source of information and the quality or veracity of the information received. No information coming from one source was considered to be fully relevant or accurate. Every information had to be cross-checked from at least two sources or more than two, including the use of technical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on the methodology used by the DB to do this cross-checking?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As for the KLA activities, yes, I can do that. Within the State Security Service in Kosovo and Metohija, in the period of time when the KLA started being active, a special operations action was organised, which is a method of work of the State Security Service based on which plans were drafted on how to penetrate that organisation and thus gain information on their activities. In that context, tasks were divided into tasks for regional centres, tasks for subcentres, and tasks for operatives who worked on the ground in the area where the KLA was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do - that is, the Service do - to corroborate or cross-reference the information to make assessments as to reliability? What sort of physical things did the Service do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically speaking, if we take just one event, we never used just reports of our associates. That is the term that we used; associates are people who covertly and in an organised way work for the State Security Service. That's the definition. They would draw up their report, reports of associates. Based on those reports, we would assess the information and using other methodology, we would cross-reference and verify that information. Based on that information, subcentres and operatives received specific tasks as to what they had to verify either because the information was incomplete or there was something else missing, so that we could gain reliable information on the person that provided this. This included the use of technical equipment, supervision or surveillance, and covert recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your statement and attached to it, you've referred to some KLA communiques. Were they -- did you use those documents as -- as your methodology to cross-reference to information you had received from informers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The basis for our work in that period of time in Kosovo and Metohija were live sources, use of technical equipment, and the Albanian media or media in Albanian language. The media in Albanian language created something that you should know about, which is the general atmosphere in the public opinion among Albanians. Given that not a lot of people speak Albanian, we realised that they published a lot of important information in Albanian language. It was especially done by this organisation called LPK. Their newspaper which was published in Switzerland was available to us one or two days after publication. That's how long it took for that newspaper to reach the analytics department where at which point in time we would start reading it and cross-referencing it with other information that we had. In addition to this, we also received information from the Public Security Service, also from the military intelligence, and from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. We also exchanged information with foreign security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the system of grading the reliability of intelligence? I mean from worthless -- or information as from worthless as to absolutely accurate or reliable? What was the system that was used and what were the gradations employed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to grading the reliability of sources, we had three categories: Source is reliable, source is partially reliable, and source is unreliable. Those were our -- that was our classification. We had a very similar grading of information pieces that we received. Information pieces were considered either fully verified, partially verified, or non-verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did it take to grade a source as "reliable" or "partially reliable"? What sort of information did you need or -- or criteria did you use to make the gradation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, now that I've mentioned a report of associates which was one of the key elements that we used in order to assess the importance of information received needed to draw forecasts, we would start from the very beginning. First we would make a basis -- a basic assessment of the person and that person's character when he was recruited to work for the Security Service. Then we followed that person, his development. And you have to know that no service in the world trusts a source fully. Even if we used a source for a long period of time, even if that source cooperated with -- with us for a long period of time - and we use the term "cooperate" in Serbia - we would still verify the information received from that associate. Some associates were trusted more; some were trusted less. But I would say that that's typical in our kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were sources or informers rewarded by the State Security?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I hate to interrupt. We've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've introduced a new concept, that's of informers. And we've been dealing with associates. I don't know whether that's a new category or not. I would like clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a difference between associates and informers and sources? If so, what is it? And then please tell us how anyone in those categories were reward?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The question was put to me concerning a report of associates. That's the terminology that we use. Various services use various terms. The State Security Service used the term "associate" to refer to such people who covertly and in an organised manner worked for the State Security Service. The other term that we used was "an operative connection," which referred to people who worked for the State Security Service but not at the level where they could be considered associates. That means that those people were monitored and were sort of groomed to become associates. As for the term "informer" or "informant," that's a typical kind of word. Some people use terms such as "sources," "agents," "insiders." People use different terms, depending on how they receive information from a live source. So in order to avoid any confusion, Your Honours, by your leave, I propose to use a term "a live source," which means that it's a human being providing information to us. I think that would avoid any further miscommunication and help us avoid confusion in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 200 people you referred to in the KLA before, are they live sources?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how were people in their category rewarded by the State Security?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The motivation of these people in their work for the State Security Service was diverse, just like anywhere else. The basic element was money. The second possible motive was of political nature, where they did not agree or they disapproved of -- of various activities. And the third motive was to compromise somebody. If somebody -- if we had information about somebody that was of compromising nature, then we would resort to blackmailing. I'm using that term because this is what it amounts to everywhere else in the world. And in this category, we are mostly dealing with partially verified information, and these people worked under a pseudonym. They would only be mentioned under a pseudonym in various reports. If you wish, we -- I can explain our methodology and tell you how we made contact with such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it assists the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it in your hands, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I anticipate that the Defence will ask the question, so I might as well get in first.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'd certainly like to hear a little bit more about the blackmail, if possible, in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Said very innocently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But please go on, Mr. Stijovic, about -- can you please explain the -- the methodology of making contact with such people.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: We would create a compromising information -- or rather, compromising documents on the activity of a certain person. If it related to the cooperation with the KLA, then that was the information that we gained about these persons directly participating in KLA activities, in crimes, in criminal activities. And given the position that these people had within the KLA -- they were quite at a high level and were able to provide very important and relevant information to us. Then based on that, we would recruit them and introduce them to the Service. We would confront them with the information that we had about the incriminating activities that they were involved in, and then we asked them to do something for us in exchange for not being prosecuted, and they would do these things under the supervision and under the control of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did that, in your professional experience, affect the assessment of the reliability of the information you received? Just -- just hang on a moment. There's an objection, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not an objection. It's simply that -- that the witness indicated in lines 23 to 25 that once confronted, the individuals would be asked to do things under the supervision and control of the State Security Service, which is obviously a different concept from the provision of information. I wonder if it might be clarified what things it was they were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it is different or not. I mean, providing information is also doing something. That's -- When you said that you then asked them to do something for us in exchange for not being prosecuted and they would do these things, what did you have in mind there? What kind of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to our instructions, they would gather, first of all, information about the KLA activities. They would also obtain certain documents for us. They would inform us about the upcoming meetings, about the contacts of the KLA members. They would provide minutes or records from their meetings. When I use the term "things," meaning things they did, I was referring to gathering information about the KLA activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you: Could doing something, could that include also changing reality? That is, forging documents, planting evidence. Or was it just that what they would do is to obtain documents, information as it existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would obtain, gather information, and nothing other than that. And I say this on the basis of everything that I have seen. They -- this involved no forging or no doctoring of anything. Nothing of that nature was done in their cooperation with the State Security Service. They worked under the control and supervision of the Security Service and it all amounted to gathering, collecting, obtaining information and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question in this respect: You earlier said when you had discovered compromising activities by these persons. Would you ever induce a compromising situation? For example, if you would find out that someone was active in the KLA, well, that could be considered compromising to the extent known to your organisation and perhaps to the police and then to prevent prosecution. That's -- that's what I understand. Could it also be that you would create a compromising situation and then blackmail that person on the basis of such compromising information? I mean, would you induce extramarital relations or something like that and then blackmail the persons involved with this compromising information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned a detail. Your Honour, I hope you want -- won't mind me repeating this. This is a detail that is being used in all security services. Immoral behaviour is one of the elements and one of the means of compromising people, by confronting people with the evidence of their behaviour and thus making them behave in accordance to your instructions. When speaking of Albanians, I have to tell you that these are patriarchal families where the authority of the head of the family is very high, and thus all of the human behaviour that has to do with immoral activities, adultery, alcohol abuse, all this is very fertile ground for having conversations with them in order to convince them to start working for the Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was, as a matter of fact, focusing. But perhaps I have not been clear enough on the following: Some people behave immorally without being encouraged to do so by others. Some need a bit of a push. Would the pushes be part of your instruments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not. Knowledge about someone's immoral behaviour, the information that we gained on that through our work was the only thing that we used. We never induced anybody to act immorally and then use it against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: With that clarification, I just return to what I was asking you a moment ago. When armed with that information of "immoral behaviour," how did that in your professional experience affect the assessment of the reliability of the information you received from those immoral-type people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The quality of such information in such an atmosphere with predominating patriarchal moral principles, when one finds out that there is a case of adultery among relatives, that there is a situation which could be of compromising nature, not only for the persons involved but also for the entire family that could lead to some very typical consequences, such as blood revenge, a blood feud which exists in Kosovo and Metohija. Then this was a very good tool for recruiting a person. And the higher the level, the greater the possibility to keep that person under the control. If somebody was drunk and had a traffic misdemeanour because of that and if we proposed to that person not to go to gaol for 30 days as a result of that but offered some benefits for them, that person could not be fully trusted. And when you receive information from such a person, then you would always treat that information with -- you would put it under scrutiny. Also, if somebody was involved in gambling and if somebody, you know, suffered great consequences because of that, then that was a possibility. Also, if somebody used drugs but not to the detrimental level, if somebody was a drug dealer, then of course you would treat the information gained from such a person with some -- you would treat it with a grain of salt. You wouldn't take it for granted. You wouldn't take it as accurate on the face of it but would rather cross-reference that information with other sources in order to be sure that the story they told you was accurate, sincere, and that information obtained through that person could be used by the Service as relevant and reliable in order to analyse the activities of that person, other persons of that organisation. You would weigh it all very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, which category of live sources gave you the most reliable information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Definitely an associate. That was the highest level of a live source providing information to the State Security Service. The level below that was an operational connection, operative connection. And the level below that was gathering information from the citizens. In accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure in my country, pursuant to Article 155 -- 151, paragraph 2, the police was authorised to conduct an interview with the person and thus obtain information that was important for us. This category was used quite a lot, and we received a lot of information from this category, but all of this information, all of this intelligence that we obtained in this way was cross-referenced with other sources. If you caught eight terrorists crossing the border illegally and smuggling weapons, then all eight of them would be interviewed about the circumstances of that event, and after gaining all of the information from them, after assessing all of that, we would gain an idea about what was going on, where the -- that activity had originated, and how it further developed. We use this category of live sources quite a lot. And based on interviews with them, we would compile an official note on interview conducted. That's what the document was officially called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just go back to the category of associates. Can you just elaborate, in case it's a little bit unclear, on exactly what an associate was within the Service and whether they were paid and, if so, how.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I have said that an associate was a person who covertly, in an organised way, and systematically gathered information for the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they -- were they on the staff of the State Security or were they being paid to work for them in another way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not employed. They were not staff members of the State Security Service. They were outside associates. And the service rewarded them. I think that that's an appropriate term to use, "rewarded" them for their work, depending on the significance of the information and the kind of information they provided. Sometimes those were regular monthly rewards and sometimes they would be rewarded just for a report, a piece of information they provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I -- just for the sake of the record, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The witness has explained a number of different motivations for individuals to be providing information: Money and blackmail, for example. Now, I had understand -- understood his testimony to -- to encompass both associates and those at the immediately -- the level immediately beneath associates. If I've misunderstood that, it would be extremely helpful to have that clarified. And secondly, in respect of the last answer that the witness has given, that the amount of a reward would depend on the significance of the information, it would be extremely helpful, again, if it could be clarified whether it follows from that that the more useful the information was perceived to be, the higher the sum of money would be paid. I appreciate these are questions that could be pursued in cross-examination, but just in order to understand the evidence in chief, it would be helpful to have them clear at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Re, we could immediately ask the witness: When you are talking about people and the motives for which they cooperated with you, associates and below, were you talking about those or were you also talking about other categories or -- you were not talking about those employed by your service, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No, that's a separate category. Associates are people who are not employed by the State Security Service. They do not receive a salary from the Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the other question was, yes, if you paid them for information they provided, would that payment be in accordance with the importance of the information or would you pay more for vital information than you'd pay for more ordinary information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Your Honour. It is trading. If the infiltrator is a highly ranked person and if that information is highly sensitive and valuable, then the monetary reward should affect the value and it is up to the commission to determine the exact amount. It can be several thousands of German marks of -- or Euro, even, depending on the importance of information and the level of that person. If we have a person who is within the inner circle, the inner-most circle - this being the Main Staff - and if that person gathers and forwards information to you once they return from abroad, you have to pay for his expenses, you have to give him a reward. Therefore, it depends on the level of infiltration and the value of information. Certain people also received regular monthly installments in addition to the irregular expenses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm unclear about one point. The gentleman said it's up to the commission to determine the exact amount. I take it there's a body that makes a determination of the amount of money to be paid to any individual who's given information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a correct understanding by Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I misspoke. A proposal for the -- for a reward is given by an operative with whom the associate is cooperating, and the decision concerning the proposal is made by the chief of the Centre of the Security Service. The operative in question was allowed to give monetary rewards up to a certain amount, but anything beyond that had to go in writing. A proposal had to be made, to which a decision would be issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re. Mr. Re, it seems that you are thinking about your next question. I'm thinking about having a break. Also because those assisting us might have been here even before we started. We'll have a break until half past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Re, the Chamber was informed that the Defence will not object to the request for an amendment of the indictment. Now, in order to speed up things, I'd -- I do understand that you do not make any application for adding witnesses to the witness list if you do not know yet whether the -- whether the amendment of the indictment will be approved. Nevertheless, the Chamber would not be opposed against you making a provisional request to add -- I think three witnesses were mentioned in the -- in the request for leave to amend the indictment. And if you would inform the Defence perhaps about the times you would need for that, and then if the Defence could respond. Even such a request, the matter is, I would say, pretty obvious that if you give more specifications that you need another type of evidence. If you would make such a provisional request orally, the Chamber would not mind. It would then be on the record. If the Defence could respond to such a provisional request, that is, in case the amendment -- the requested leave to amend the indictment would be granted, then the Prosecution would like to add to the witness list the Witness A, B, and C, and if the Defence could respond to that or tell the Chamber whether it opposes such a request, then we can speed up matters and not lose any time. Mr. Re, you may proceed. Mr. Stijovic, this had nothing to do with you, but it was a tiny procedural issue I had to raise. But now we focus again, and we'll carefully listen to your testimony. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the break, we were talking -- we were talking about the categories of people who provided information to the DB. What I want to find out is was there a way of working out from the documents, including those which are annexed to your statement, which category of people have given you the information in those documents? That is, associate, or operative source, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what -- what's that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In order to assess a document received through a live source --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, interpreter's correction, on the basis of documents received through live sources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the basis of reports that I mentioned that are attached to the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: More specifically, is there something on the face of the document that will tell us instantly the category of source for that document? That is, whether it's from an associate or a -- an operative or whatever.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: There is such an indication at the top of the document, and also one can gather that from the type of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is the indication at the top that tells us where -- the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the information received through associates, the template and the form in which information is shared are specified in the document under the heading "Associate report." As regards operational connections and the persons that the Service had conducted an interview with, based on Article 151, subparagraph 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, that document is called "Note on an interview conducted, official note." There is a template which contains data on the source, and it is clearly specified what kind of source that is and what is the degree of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are 78 documents in the binder in front of you. Would you be able to find relatively easily something -- an example in the category of associate report? And if you can, just refer to which annex the document is and we'll take it from there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is not a problem. However, I may have some difficulty finding it in the file. I will eventually come across an associate report. There it is. It is binder -- just a second, please. 48. Tab 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that is 65 ter 2 --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: 48, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 65 ter Exhibit 2034.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can that document remain under seal at the moment, as it contains the name of, I think, a live source, as it's been termed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I may be wrong, but I think it's anonymised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's the document dated the 16th of April, 1998, and in English it says "Report of a collaborator."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Emmerson, I do not see that it's anonymised. I see the first line under 1 -- well, a number and a name which might be a nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even there I would be very careful with nicknames. Often nicknames are related one way or another with real names.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour will see there's quite a large number of these reports which appear to contain code names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's be -- let's stay on the safe side at this moment. Yes, it should remain under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, could that get a number before we move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will P932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, without mentioning the name of the person who's described as a collaborator --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. Excuse me. Before we go any further, since it is an annex, we have a standing objection to all annexes. I don't know how the Chamber wishes to treat that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that we'll not determine the matter at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We need more time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, I don't know at this moment what type of questions will be. And since the Defence has made, on several occasions, a distinction between the reason for admission. Whether the Chamber could do so is another matter. But let's just wait and see. But it's on the record that you oppose the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for purposes just of some guidance, would the Chamber at this time like that each time we're dealing with an annex for us to make a specific objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you now object against all the annexes, then that's on the record. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one qualification to that, obviously: It is objection to those annexes to which objection is taken in the motion. There are some annexes which do not fall within that category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- the response -- no, the motion. No, the motion. The annexes to -- the annexes to the motion where you set out exactly this one, paragraph so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I do see that you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, I wish it to be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You list clearly in your motion --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's supplemental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Not alternative. So I join with Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's objection, unless contradicted by the presence or the absence, the presence of a non-objection or the absence of an objection in your motions. Yes, that's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name of the collaborator, is that a nickname or a name given to the person by the service for the purposes of identifying them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: In the first part where there is data on the information source, it says: "Associate Jaglic." Jaglic was a pseudonym used internally. It was used in internal correspondence within the RDB. Next to the number -- next to the pseudonym there is a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Re. Out of an abundance of caution, I said that it should be under seal, because of the mentioning of the pseudonym. What's your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, maybe the witness can tell us. If it -- if it's harmless and it's an internal thing which doesn't -- doesn't identify, I'm comfortable. But if it's a name which could identify the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have some concerns that the pseudonym could identify the person? No. You say there's no risk. So we could use that name without any further protection of that person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you this: Even the person concerned does not know his pseudonym. It has nothing to do with his name. It's a code name given to the person by the operative who contacted him or her. This was simply a code name used internally. I cannot tell you whether it can put the person in any danger. I can only tell you there is no relation. The pseudonym has nothing to do with the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's about the name. Now, the content of the report could be of a nature which might identify that person. I don't know. I haven't read it yet. If you have any concerns in that respect, then we leave the document under seal. And I leave it to Mr. Re to find the right moment to go into private session. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Might we establish, please, simply "yes" or "no," not with a substantive answer, whether the witness himself knows the identity of the person who is referred to by this pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's ask the witness. You've just named that person by his pseudonym. Do you personally know that person for which a pseudonym is introduced here? Have you met him? Do you know who he is? I'm not asking who -- who it is but I'm asking whether you know who he is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would publishing the information in this report, in your view, lead to the danger of identifying who the person is? If the contents became known, could that person's identity be exposed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps out of caution, we should go into private session as soon as you start asking questions of a character that go to the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the form of this document as one which you can use to identify those provided by an operative. What is it about this document which enables you to tell the Trial Chamber that this is information provided by a -- I think you said "associate" before. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. In any serious analysis or having conducted such an analysis, one could realise who the person is. In item 2, we have data on enemy activity; meaning that that person addressed the structure, position, and location of various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not making myself clear. All I want to know is: Looking at the document, what enables you to work out from what's written at the top, the -- the name for the collaborator, the number, things which are written on it, "OO", "PO", et cetera, to tell you this is a report made from an associate, as opposed to a different type of live source? The question is just based on the format of the document and what's on it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This is an authentic document from the RDB. It was drafted by an operative of the RDB who had contact with the associate. The authenticity can easily be verified if one looks at the left upper corner, where it clearly states whose document it is: "The Republic of Serbia. Ministry of the Interior, State Security Service, Albanian extremism and terrorism. RDB centre Prizren, RDB office Pec." Below that is a code, and that is the operative's number. Below there is the date of drafting, and in the right-hand corner one can read that the data forwarded by the associate have to do with the operative action Krug, "circle," and concerns various people that the RDB conducted investigations into. And I mean by this that the acronyms "OO" and "PO" reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence earlier was the most reliable information came from associates, as opposed to those lower down on the categories you described, operatives, et cetera. What is it about looking at the document that enables you to say -- that this relates to an operative -- sorry, an associate? What's the code or the -- or the template or the key which says this is an associate's report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the first part of the document of an associate report looks like this. The first item contains data on the source of information. This is what we use when reporting. Below that, we have a description of what it concerns. It says here clearly: "Associate Jaglic." This is the form, standard form, and all of the data mentioned here has to be there in this type of document, and it should also describe what the report of the associate has to do with and the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, there might be a translation issue. The word used translated in English as "collaborator," the original being "saradnika" we'd like to hear from our interpreters whether "saradnika" is a collaborator or could also be translated or also translated as an associate. I'm listening to the English channel at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The words are synonymous. However; as of the beginning of the trial today, we used the term "associate," so we kept using the same word so as to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the word used by the witness earlier when he spoke about an associate is the same word that we find here, that is "saradnika".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. This being clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I take advantage of that pause to ask whether Mr. Re can clarify with the witness again with a yes or no rather an a content response whether in respect of this report and other similar reports the witness himself knows what the operative's code - 0389 in this instance - indicates. In other words, whether he knows the identity of the operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He just said he did. He said he knew the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No. No, Mr. Re. I think I asked him whether he personally knew the person that was given a pseudonym in this report. I think that Mr. Emmerson is now inquiring into the number of the operative, that is 04845 just below "RDB Pec Detachment." I think that's where the witness said the code of the employee -- that's -- looking at this number -- I'm not asking you who it is. But this person by his number 04845, would you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, concerning this associate report, the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly that you say perhaps I would not know for others, but this one I know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely correct. This was one of the most important and it was a quality source for the surface. Therefore, we valued his reports. And by the virtue of my position, I know who the person is. By your leave, Your Honour, I do not understand English, but I -- what I can see on the screen before me is "collaborator," and I believe it is a translation matter. An associate is an associate. A collaborator in our terminology has a different connotation, in Serbian at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that "collaboration" has a negative connotation; whereas, you wanted to -- the matter has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that raises a --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure that the matter has been clarified. I think that the witness's answer, as I understand it, is repeating the answer that he gave before about personally knowing who Jaglic is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood. I gave him the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But the answer refers to the source, rather than the operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- let me then go back to what the witness said about this number. Let me just -- one second, please. I have to ... Mr. Emmerson, the witness explained the letterhead. I'm just trying to find it. Below that, Mr. Emmerson, I take you to page 38, line -- no, page 39, line 25. He first explains a few lines before that whose document it is, Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, State Security Service, Albanian extremist and terrorism, RDB centre Prizren, RDB office Pec. And then below that is a code.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the operative's number. I do understand, but let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There are, of course, two numbers below that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- seek for clarification the operative that, is not the associate but that's the person who wrote this report - Is that correctly understood? - wrote this report having received information from the person whose pseudonym appears a bit further down? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you also know the identity of the operative, not only of the person mentioned by pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, when it comes to the report of associate Jaglic, the answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a little earlier that "this was one of the most important and was a quality source for the Service, therefore we valued his reports." Are you referring to the operative or Jaglic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the associate Jaglic, not the operative. The associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was it about Jaglic's reports that gave them this high level of quality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I don't know what the answer will be, but wouldn't it be wise to go into private session at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would -- would your answer say something that might endanger the identity of Jaglic? If so, we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, no reason for that. I don't think I'll make a mistake that would endanger him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that basis, please answer very carefully.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The said person under pseudonym "Jaglic" is a person who over a longer period of time provided information to the State Security Service about the activities of the terrorist KLA both within the country and the activities in the Albanian diaspora overseas related to the promotion of the KLA. I hope this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What enabled you to assess his or her information as quality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The information provided by this person initially helped us a great deal establish who inspired and organised the KLA and who was involved in their activities overseas. Overseas initially and later on in the country as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this person a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How was his information cross-checked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: We cross-checked them through other associates. We checked them by exchanging information with foreign services. We also checked this by using technical equipment, by using surveillance or monitoring in relation to some persons whom we were able to put under surveillance covertly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When -- when you say that, are you giving evidence about things you know from personal experience in relation to Jaglic, or are you referring generally to what the service did in cross-checking?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Since right now we spoke about Jaglic, I spoke on the basis of my personal experience and the experience that the State Security Service had with him. And generally speaking, we cross-checked information we received from anyone, including associates, regardless of how reliable that person was considered or how -- what was the quality of the cooperation with that person until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to the format of the document. You've told us that 04845 was the code for an operative. Handwritten on the document underneath that is "0389" and also "02021" a bit to the right of that. To what do those two handwritten numbers refer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The first number is the registration number in the record books kept by the Security Service. That means that it was registered under this number. The other number, 2021, is the number that the document was kept under in the Prizren RDB. So the first number is the number of the subcentre; whereas, 2021 is the number assigned by the regional centre in Prizren in the registration books or record books.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your statement, you refer to what "OA Krug" means, and I'll come to that in a moment. Underneath that are the letters "OO" with inverted commas around them, and under that the letters "PO" in inverted commas. It's on the right-hand side of the front page. What do they refer to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I -- both "OA," "OO," and "PO," are kinds of operations work of the State Security Service during that period of time. Operations action is a complex type of operative work that enables the Security Service to use various measures and live sources in relation to a certain person or an event that was of interest for us. There was a deadline for the completion of that action envisaged. As for "OO," that stands for "operativna obrada", which is a level below operations action, and it means that certain persons were put under operative measures. That's what it stands for. It simply has to do with the kind of measures that are applied in relation to a certain person, measures or different kinds of work of our service in relation to that person. Let me just add this: It also means that the information provided by this person refers both to persons included in previous reports, persons that are covered by operative measures, and persons that are covered by operative actions. So these are all different kinds of work or measures applied by the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's just divide it in two: The first one "OO". Can you just said the word slowly so we can get a translation of what it is into English.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: "OO" stands for operativna obrada. As for "PO" --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the translators or the interpreters interpret for us what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be it didn't appear translated on the transcript. Therefore Mr. Re is seeking the English for obrada.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Operations measure or operative measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: OP, just can you -- sorry, "PO," what's that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: "PO" stands for predhodna obrada, which is initial measure. Let me describe an example. For example, the State Security Service learns that there is hostile activity in a certain area. This is the first piece of information. That means that something is going on that is of interest to the service. If the service receives several pieces of such information in a short period of time indicating that there is a certain person or a certain group dealing -- or rather, involved in this activity, then this person or this group is covered by "PO," by initial measures. This is the kind of measures that are applied in relation to that person or group. As the time goes by, if the information about the activities of that person or group escalates and becomes more relevant to the service, then the initial measures are stepped up and become operative measures. As for operative actions, that is a higher level of work including measures that are more complex against the person or group that had been initially put under initial measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On the document, in the heading on the left, the fourth line, it says: "III/AET." What does "III" mean and what does "AET" stand for. And can you just say it slowly so we can interpret what "AET" means.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: The State Security Service organised its work on the principle of territorial and professional work. This "III" stands for third professional work, which in our service dealt with extremists. Under extremists, we had Albanian extremists and terrorists, Serbian extremists and terrorists, and Muslim extremists and terrorists and their activities. To put it briefly, this line of work dealt with internal security. We also had the first professional line of work and the second professional line of work. If you're not interested in that, we don't need to speak of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "AET," what's that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: That's an acronym which stands for "Albanian extremism and terrorism."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, we find that already on page 39, line 24, where the witness explained the letterhead. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to the five-digit code "04845", did every operative have a five-digit code?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: I personally had a five-digit code. This had to do with the computer and technical service, in order to compress the information and to protect operatives. I think that all officers who were authorised operatives had a five-digit code that stood for their name and other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a master list somewhere matching the digits -- digit codes to their names?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A number of these -- a number of these documents bear five-digit codes. Do you from memory know the -- know the identities of the people whose digit code -- five-digit codes appear in these documents? I mean, do you know them all or some of them, is what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that question already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked him if he would know this one. He said, "This one, I would know." Then I said, "Would I correctly understand you that you don't know them all but this one you know?" And he said, "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the documents he has, not -- not everyone in the whole service. I'm just referring to the documents annexed to his statement, whether he knows the identity of those in these statements. It's a shortcut. I think Your Honour's question was referring to the -- I understood it to be referring to the whole or generally to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, so you're now talking about all the five-digit numbers in all the documents attached? That was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that was your question, then that has not been answered. I fully agree with you. But I didn't understand that to be the question. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, could I try to -- to seek -- You've seen the annexes to your statement. Among them, a lot of reports by operatives, all under a five-digit number. From those documents, do you know all of these operatives? Do you recognise them on the basis of their five-digit number? Or do you know only some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
